Cypriot television networks may face fierce competition from a planned new Russian-language channel which could attract a considerable number of advertisers.
Even though no formal complaint has yet been submitted to the Cyprus Broadcasting Authority, there is a lot of behind-the-scenes pressure on authorities to drop the condition of Greek subtitles in Russian-language broadcasts. In this way, they hope to limit the Russian channel’s number of viewers and hence the interest of Cypriot businesses in advertising.
The Russian-language channel has only recently secured a temporary broadcast licence, subject to the rule that its broadcasts will have Greek subtitles. This term was applied because the Cyprus Radio Television Authority needed to be able control the channel’s broadcasts without hiring additional personnel fluent in Russian.
This channel’s licence, as well the licences of all other non-subscription channels in Cyprus, expired on 30 June 2018. The Cyprus Radio Television Authority is currently reviewing applications submitted for new temporary licences which will be valid until 30 June 2019.
Shareholders of the company behind the creation and operation of the Russian-language channel network were willing to abide with the directives of the Cyprus Broadcasting Authority from the start and have already approached companies with relevant experience in subtitling.
According to sources, members of the Board of Directors of Cyprus Broadcasting Authority are considering withdrawing the demand for subtitles. Overall, it appears that the broadcasting Authority is heading towards a partial withdrawal of the term: in particular, it is probable that some of the broadcasts and not all of them will be subtitled.
rewrite:
Cypriot television networks could soon face intense competition from a planned Russian-language channel, which may draw a significant share of advertisers. While no formal complaint has yet been lodged with the Cyprus Broadcasting Authority, there is considerable behind-the-scenes pressure on regulators to remove the requirement for Greek subtitles on Russian-language broadcasts. Opponents hope that by doing so, they can limit the channel’s viewership and reduce its appeal to local businesses for advertising.

The Russian-language channel recently obtained a temporary broadcast license, conditional on including Greek subtitles. This rule was imposed so the Cyprus Radio Television Authority could monitor the channel’s content without needing to hire additional Russian-speaking staff. The license for this channel, along with all other non-subscription channels in Cyprus, expired on June 30, 2018. The Authority is now reviewing applications for new temporary licenses, which would be valid until June 30, 2019.

From the outset, shareholders of the company behind the Russian-language channel have expressed willingness to comply with the Authority’s directives and have already contacted firms with expertise in subtitling. According to sources, members of the Broadcasting Authority’s board are now considering dropping the subtitle requirement. Overall, it appears the Authority is moving toward a partial relaxation of the rule—likely requiring subtitles only for some broadcasts, rather than all.

input: Looks like Mayor Fred Eisenberger's puppy, Dash, will have a new friend to visit when he heads to work with the mayor this summer. Pictured here is Ralph, the creation of the City of Hamilton's horticultural staff. The approximately 15-foot sculpture was developed using Carex buchananii (leatherleaf sedge), a sage grass native to New Zealand and grown in the city greenhouses this spring. The grasses were rooted into a frame created by local metal artist Trevor McInytre with the internal infrastructure designed and implemented by the horticultural staff. This includes soil and a watering system inside the sculpture to keep Ralph's "fur" healthy and growing throughout the hot summer. The whimsical garden's designs were initiated by Marcia Monaghan, superintendent of horticulture for the city. She says her inspiration came from seeing Mosaic Culture, a huge horticultural display in Ottawa last year. Monaghan says that despite all the significant dog references — including the mayor's dog, the OHL-winning Bulldogs and the fact that it is the Year of the Dog in Chinese culture — none of these were actually the inspiration for the sculpture. Monaghan says, "We just thought it would be fun." The gardens, which also include a huge butterfly, will be completed midday Friday.
rewrite:
Mayor Fred Eisenberger’s puppy, Dash, will soon have a new companion to visit when accompanying the mayor to work this summer. Meet Ralph, a whimsical sculpture crafted by the City of Hamilton’s horticultural team. Standing about 15 feet tall, Ralph is made from Carex buchananii, or leatherleaf sedge—a sage grass native to New Zealand that was grown in the city’s greenhouses this spring. The grasses were rooted into a metal frame created by local artist Trevor McInytre, while the horticultural staff designed the internal structure, complete with soil and an integrated watering system to keep Ralph’s “fur” lush and healthy through the summer heat.

The garden design was initiated by Marcia Monaghan, the city’s superintendent of horticulture, who drew inspiration from seeing Mosaic Culture, a large horticultural display in Ottawa last year. Although the sculpture coincides with several dog-related themes—from the mayor’s own pup to the OHL-winning Bulldogs and the Chinese Year of the Dog—Monaghan clarifies that none of these directly inspired the project. “We just thought it would be fun,” she says. The gardens, which also feature a large butterfly, are set to be completed by midday Friday.

VICTORIA — Here are questions Attorney General David Eby has recommended to cabinet for a referendum this fall on British Columbia’s electoral system:
1. Which should British Columbia use for elections to the legislative assembly (Vote for only one):
— The current first-past-the post voting system.
— A proportional representation voting system.
2. If British Columbia adopts a proportional representation voting system, which of the following voting systems do you prefer? (Vote for the voting systems you wish to support by ranking them in order of preference. You may choose to support one, two or all three of the systems):
— Dual-member proportional.
— Mixed-member proportional.
— Rural-urban.
——
Here is a look at the three systems of proportional representation that have been recommended:
— Dual-member proportional would take most of the province’s existing single-member electoral districts and amalgamate them with a second neighbouring district to create two-member districts. The largest rural districts could remain unchanged as single-member districts. Parties could nominate up to two candidates in each district. They would appear on the ballot in an order determined by the party. The first seats would be won by the first candidates of the party that received the most votes in each electoral district. The second seats would be allocated based on provincewide voting results and individual district results.
— A mixed-member system would combine single-member electoral districts, where members are elected under first past the post, with seats also allocated on a regional or provincial level and based on a list of candidates running for proportional representation seats prepared by the parties.
— A rural-urban option is also a mixed system that elects members of the legislature two ways. In urban and semi-urban areas, a single transferable vote would be used to rank candidates by preference. In rural areas, single-member electoral districts would elect their representative using the first-past-the-post system, while a small number of proportional representation seats would also be allocated from a list prepared by the parties based on election results.
rewrite:
VICTORIA — Attorney General David Eby has presented cabinet with proposed questions for a referendum this fall on changing British Columbia’s electoral system. The recommended questions are as follows:

1. Which electoral system should British Columbia use for elections to the legislative assembly? (Vote for only one):
   — The current first-past-the-post voting system.
   — A proportional representation voting system.

2. If British Columbia adopts a proportional representation voting system, which of the following specific systems do you prefer? (Rank your preferred systems in order. You may choose to rank one, two, or all three options):
   — Dual-member proportional.
   — Mixed-member proportional.
   — Rural-urban proportional.

Here is an overview of the three proportional representation systems under consideration:

— **Dual-member proportional** would merge most of the province’s existing single-member ridings with a neighboring district to form two-member districts, though the largest rural ridings could stay as single-member districts. Parties could nominate up to two candidates per district, listed on the ballot in a party-determined order. The first seat in each district would go to the leading candidate of the party that receives the most votes. The second seat would then be allocated based on both provincewide and local voting results to improve overall proportionality.

— **Mixed-member proportional** combines single-member districts—elected through first-past-the-post—with additional seats filled from party lists at a regional or provincial level. These list seats are allocated to ensure that each party’s total share of seats better reflects its share of the popular vote.

— **The rural-urban proportional** model is also a mixed system. In urban and semi-urban areas, voters would use a single transferable vote to rank candidates by preference. In rural areas, representatives would be elected from single-member districts using first-past-the-post, supplemented by a limited number of proportional seats allocated from party lists to balance the overall results.

eClinicalWorks launches telehealth solution on healow mobile app
eClinicalWorks, a provider of healthcare IT solutions, has made its telehealth solution available on its Health & Online Wellness (healow) mobile app.
This service will provide patients with live video visits.
The TeleVisits feature has been integrated within the eClinicalWorks electronic health records (EHR) Platform.
All information, submitted or shared by patients using this solution, can be imported into the HER, which in turn supports workflow, clinical research and boosts patient satisfaction as they will have access to care whenever and wherever it is required.
Further, telehealth is becoming mainstream, several providers are making investments in third-party services instead of offering it as a standard service integrated with the practice’s existing technology.
This in turn leaves patients with the trouble of downloading additional apps, remembering login information and then experiencing the inconvenience of not having their telehealth summaries linked with their personal health records.
healow TeleVisits offers a seamless experience for patients and providers with EHR integration being in place.
eClinicalWorks CEO and co-founder Girish Navani said: “healow TeleVisits for the smartphone is taking telehealth to a whole new level by making healthcare more accessible.
“In today’s digital health age, patients are interested in care solutions that offer quicker delivery and flexibility. Additionally, providers are seeing benefits with increased patient engagement and streamlined workflow.”
eClinicalWorksis a privately held firm. Its solutions are used by more than 125,000 physicians and nurse practitioners. Among the customers include ACOs, physician practices, hospitals, community health centers, departments of health, and convenient care clinics.
Headquartered in Westborough, Massachusetts, eClinicalWorks has offices in Austin, New York City, Chicago, California, Georgia, London, India, and Dubai.

Breaking News Emails Get breaking news alerts and special reports. The news and stories that matter, delivered weekday mornings. SUBSCRIBE
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court ruled Tuesday that thousands of victims of terrorist attacks overseas cannot sue a foreign bank under a U.S. law dating from the 1700s.
By a 5-4 vote, the court refused to revive lawsuits, dismissed by the lower courts, that sought to hold Arab Bank, which is headquartered in Jordan, responsible for attacks against foreign nationals in the Middle East. More than 6,000 survivors and relatives of those killed in the West Bank and Gaza claimed that officials of the bank were complicit in the attacks.
Beginning in 2004, the victims filed a series of lawsuits accusing the bank of helping to finance Hamas and other terror organizations. The legal action was filed in the U.S. and aimed at Arab Bank through its branch in New York. The lead plaintiff in the case before the Supreme Court, Joseph Jesner, lost his 19-year-old son to a suicide bombing in Tel Aviv.
The lawsuits invoked one of the first laws ever passed by Congress, the Alien Tort Statute of 1789, known as ATS, intended to be a forum for resolving claims of piracy. But Tuesday's ruling said the law did not allow lawsuits of the kind filed by the terror victims.
"Absent further action from Congress, it would be inappropriate for courts to extend ATS liability to foreign corporations," wrote Justice Anthony Kennedy for the court's majority.
"Courts are not well suited to make the required policy judgments that are implicated by corporate liability in cases like this one."

More than 6,000 survivors and family members of those killed in the West Bank and Gaza had alleged that bank officials were complicit in the violence.

The legal actions began in 2004, with victims filing a series of suits accusing the bank of helping to finance Hamas and other terrorist groups. These cases were brought in the United States, targeting Arab Bank through its New York branch. Among the plaintiffs was Joseph Jesner, who lost his 19-year-old son in a Tel Aviv suicide bombing and served as the lead plaintiff in the Supreme Court case.

However, Tuesday’s ruling clarified that this law does not permit the type of claims filed by the terror victims. Writing for the majority, Justice Anthony Kennedy stated, "Absent further action from Congress, it would be inappropriate for courts to extend ATS liability to foreign corporations." He added, "Courts are not well suited to make the required policy judgments that are implicated by corporate liability in cases like this one."

SYRACUSE, N.Y. – It goes without saying that when you order something custom-made, you expect to receive exactly what you imagine.
However, for Malexa Maeweather, an 18-year-old from Syracuse, New York, a made-to-order prom dress had some unexpected and disastrous results.
According to Seventeen Magazine, Maeweather reached out to a local designer, Kia Wagner, in the hopes that she could create a one-of-a-kind prom dress. Instead, she said she got an absolute dress fail. Even worse, Maeweather didn’t get to see the dress until the night before prom.
Maeweather told WGN, “I was so upset and very aggravated. I didn’t know what I was going to do.”
It wasn’t just Maeweather who was disappointed with the results of the dress. In fact, Maeweather’s mother, Dee Lewis, told Seventeen that Wagner never updated her daughter on the progress of the dress, which left the teen in tears when it finally arrived. Having already put down a $100 downpayment for the dress priced at $300, Lewis took to Facebook to express her discontent.
“So Kia Wagner called my daughter Malexa Maeweather THE NIGHT before prom to pick up her dress which she charges $300 for. Are you serious…was I wrong for wanting my DEPOSIT BACK.”
In response to Lewis, Wagner also posted on Facebook stating, “the reason [Lewis] will not get her $100 deposit back is because I was simply following the instructions she agreed and decided to she had a variety of fabric selections to choose from and as well as several of fittings where i asked her numerous of times if this was the look she was going for…”
Nevertheless, with help from her mother and close friends, Maeweather was able to find and purchase a new dress to salvage her prom day.

Compounding the frustration, Maeweather did not see the dress until the night before prom. “I was so upset and very aggravated. I didn’t know what I was going to do,” she told WGN.

The disappointment extended to her family. Maeweather’s mother, Dee Lewis, told Seventeen that Wagner provided no updates on the dress’s progress, leaving her daughter in tears when it finally arrived. Having already paid a $100 deposit toward the $300 total, Lewis took to Facebook to voice her frustration. She wrote, “So Kia Wagner called my daughter Malexa Maeweather THE NIGHT before prom to pick up her dress… Are you serious…was I wrong for wanting my DEPOSIT BACK.”

Wagner responded on Facebook, defending her position: “the reason [Lewis] will not get her $100 deposit back is because I was simply following the instructions she agreed and decided to… she had a variety of fabric selections to choose from and as well as several of fittings where i asked her numerous of times if this was the look she was going for…”

Despite the setback, Maeweather, with help from her mother and friends, managed to find and purchase a new dress in time, salvaging her prom night.

* Stocks lower on signs Fed may cut balance sheet this yr
* Automakers and banks underperform
* Defense firm Ishikawa Seisakusho soars on N.Korea concerns
By Ayai Tomisawa
TOKYO, April 6 Japan's Nikkei share average tumbled to a four-month low on Thursday morning after U.S. shares tumbled overnight on signs the U.S. Federal Reserve may start cutting its king-sized balance sheet earlier than expected.
The Nikkei dropped 1.4 percent to 18,595.12 points by the midday break, the lowest since early December.
Investors were spooked by minutes of the Fed's last meeting, which showed most policymakers thought the U.S. central bank should begin trimming its $4.5 trillion balance sheet this year.
The minutes also showed "some participants viewed equity prices as quite high relative to standard valuation measures."
"We were hit by a bucket of cold water," said Norihiro Fujito, senior investment strategist at Mitsubishi UFJ Morgan Stanley Securities.
"Signs that the Fed could pare its balance sheet is shocking enough, but the mood was exacerbated as the Fed touched upon stock valuations, which is very rare," he added.
Automakers, which were already under pressure after weak March U.S. auto sales this week, extended their decline after the dollar fell 0.3 percent at 110.390 yen. Toyota Motor Corp dropped 0.9 percent and Nissan Motor Co Ltd tumbled 1.5 percent.
Banking stocks also lost ground, with Mizuho Financial Group Inc slipping 2.0 percent and Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group Inc shedding 1.4 percent.
Investors were also wary ahead of a potentially tense meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping, the first between the world's two most powerful leaders.
Meanwhile, defence equipment maker Ishikawa Seisakusho Ltd soared 15 percent to a daily limit high of 1,137 yen, the highest level since July 2015. Investors believe demand for the company's defence equipment could surge as concerns escalate over North Korea.
Regional tensions have risen after North Korea test-fired a ballistic missile on Wednesday, just a day before the Trump-Xi summit, where North Korea's arms development drive will take centre stage.
The broader Topix dropped 1.1 percent to 1,488.39 and the JPX-Nikkei Index 400 declined 1.1 percent to 13,327.02.
(Editing by Randy Fabi)
rewrite:
Japan's Nikkei share average fell to a four-month low in morning trading on Thursday, tracking an overnight plunge on Wall Street. The drop came amid signs the U.S. Federal Reserve could start reducing its massive balance sheet sooner than anticipated. By the midday break, the Nikkei was down 1.4 percent at 18,595.12 points, its weakest level since early December.

Market sentiment was rattled by the minutes from the Fed's latest policy meeting, which revealed that a majority of officials believe the central bank should begin trimming its $4.5 trillion balance sheet sometime this year. Adding to the concern, the minutes noted that "some participants viewed equity prices as quite high relative to standard valuation measures."

"We were hit by a bucket of cold water," said Norihiro Fujito, senior investment strategist at Mitsubishi UFJ Morgan Stanley Securities. "The possibility of the Fed reducing its balance sheet is shocking enough, but the mood worsened because the Fed rarely comments directly on stock valuations."

Automakers, already under pressure from disappointing U.S. sales figures for March, extended their losses as the dollar weakened against the yen. Toyota Motor Corp fell 0.9 percent, while Nissan Motor Co Ltd dropped 1.5 percent. Banking shares also declined, with Mizuho Financial Group Inc down 2.0 percent and Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group Inc losing 1.4 percent.

Investors remained cautious ahead of a high-stakes meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, the first face-to-face discussion between the two leaders. The summit is expected to address rising tensions over North Korea, which test-fired a ballistic missile on Wednesday.

In a contrasting move, shares of defense contractor Ishikawa Seisakusho Ltd surged 15 percent to hit a daily limit high of 1,137 yen, a peak not seen since July 2015. The jump reflected investor expectations that regional security concerns would boost demand for the company's defense products.

The broader Topix index fell 1.1 percent to 1,488.39, while the JPX-Nikkei Index 400 also declined 1.1 percent to 13,327.02.

The Sports Authority of India (SAI) is set for an overhaul with Sports minister Rajyavardhan Singh Rathore announcing change in its name. Now SAI will be called Sports India. The minister also announced some structural changes in the body along with an increase in the daily food expenses of the athletes.
Sports Minister Rajyavardhan Singh Rathore on Wednesday announced that the Sports Authority of India (SAI) will be renamed. While it was not an official announcement, Rathore said that it will be called as Sports India, for the time being.
The minister also announced structural changes in the body along with an increase in the daily food expenses of the athletes.
“It’ll be made leaner, some posts won’t be retained after officers on them retire. Daily expenses of food for athletes are being raised, for which committee is also being formed,” Rathore was quoted by ANI as saying.
Last year in August 2017, the minister had said that the government was planning to change the name of the authority. He had said that there is no need for authority in sports as it’s all about service.
On being asked about the sports quota, Rathore said that the government was in favour for a minimum quota to be fixed for sportspersons. According to reports, he further said that Olympic-winning sports stars should be given reservation in ‘Grade A’ jobs.”
Rathore, who is himself an Olympic medalist, said that Centre was aiming to make the organisation more ‘lean and professional’ by reducing its strength by around 50 percent by 2022. He added that the Centre was also planning to come out with measures to expand its search for talent across the country and government wants to work towards developing a culture of sports among school students.
The SAI was established back in 1984 adn was registered as a Society under Socities Act in pursuance of the Resolution of 1984 of the Departments of Sports with the only objective of promotion of Sports and Games in the country.
SAI comes under the authority of Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports. The Ministry was set up as the Department of Sports in 1982 at the time of IX Asian Games in New Delhi.

rewrite:
In a move signaling significant reform, the Sports Authority of India (SAI) is poised for a major transformation. Sports Minister Rajyavardhan Singh Rathore announced on Wednesday that the organization will be renamed "Sports India," a change intended to reflect a shift in philosophy from an "authority" to a service-oriented body. While this is not yet an official decree, the minister indicated this will be its working name for the foreseeable future.

Accompanying the rebranding are substantive structural and operational changes. Minister Rathore, an Olympic medalist himself, stated the goal is to make the organization "leaner and more professional," with plans to reduce its workforce by approximately fifty percent by 2022. This will be achieved by not refilling certain posts after officers retire. Furthermore, in a direct benefit to athletes, the daily food allowance is being increased, and a dedicated committee is being formed to oversee this enhancement.

The minister also addressed broader sports policy, expressing the government's support for establishing a minimum job quota for sportspersons. He specifically suggested that Olympic medal winners should receive reservations in 'Grade A' government positions. These reforms are part of a larger vision to cultivate a robust sports culture nationwide. The Centre plans to implement measures to widen the talent search across the country and focus on developing sporting interest among school students.

The push for change is not new; Minister Rathore had initially mentioned the potential name change in August 2017, arguing that sports is about service, not authority. Established in 1984 and registered under the Societies Act, SAI was created with the sole objective of promoting sports and games in India. It operates under the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports, which originated as the Department of Sports in 1982 during the lead-up to the IX Asian Games in New Delhi. The current announcements mark a concerted effort to modernize this decades-old institution for a new era of Indian athletics.

TOURISM DOWN: There is trouble brewing for tourism in Agnes Water and Seventeen Seventy.
CONCERNS over a significant drop in tourism numbers at Agnes Water and Seventeen Seventy will be one of the key focuses at Gladstone Regional Council's general meeting today.
Over the last 18 months the two coastal towns have been impacted by a decrease in tourists visiting, with tourism operators holding three interlinked issues responsible:
Sand collecting in Round Hill Creek, reducing access
A lack of marina facilities to facilitate trips to the reef
A lack of reef operators capable of taking passengers
Gladstone Area Promotion and Development Limited CEO Darryl Branthwaite said the issues added up to one major problem.
"The access through Round Hill Creek is very limited for marine operators, and access is 75% of the problem here,” Mr Branthwaite said.
"Agnes Water and Seventeen Seventy have been really affected for a lengthy period of time with less reef operators going to Lady Musgrave,” he said.
Mr Branthwaite said Gladstone Regional Council had to intervene as the access situation "needs to be dramatically improved and quickly”.
A Gladstone Regional Council spokesperson said dredging at Round Hill Creek would be considered at today's council meeting.
Problems with dredging, however, include the expense and the risk the sand builds up when weather conditions change.
Discovery Coast Tourism and Commerce president Amber Rodgers said even if the creek was dredged today, tourist rates would not improve overnight.
"The reality is council are not going to go buy a new boat if access is improved. That's up to investors,” she said.
"The huge investment depends on a lot of people and the fact is, right now, we are seeing how having less seats going to the reef is affecting the rest of our businesses.”
rewrite:
Tourism in the coastal towns of Agnes Water and Seventeen Seventy is facing significant challenges, which will be a key topic at today's Gladstone Regional Council meeting. Over the past year and a half, both locations have seen a notable decline in visitor numbers. Local tourism operators point to three interconnected issues driving the downturn: sand accumulation in Round Hill Creek is restricting boat access, there is a lack of marina facilities to support trips to the reef, and too few reef tour operators are available to take passengers.

Darryl Branthwaite, CEO of Gladstone Area Promotion and Development Limited, states that these factors combine into one major problem. "Access through Round Hill Creek is very limited for marine operators, and access accounts for about 75% of the issue here," he explained. "Agnes Water and Seventeen Seventy have been significantly affected for a long time by having fewer reef operators traveling to Lady Musgrave Island." Branthwaite emphasized that the Gladstone Regional Council must step in, as the access situation "needs to be dramatically improved, and quickly."

A council spokesperson confirmed that dredging Round Hill Creek will be considered at the meeting. However, such a project faces hurdles, including high costs and the risk of sand quickly building up again if weather conditions shift. Amber Rodgers, president of Discovery Coast Tourism and Commerce, notes that even immediate dredging would not lead to an instant recovery in tourist numbers. "The reality is that the council isn't going to purchase a new boat if access improves. That's up to investors," she said. "A major investment depends on many stakeholders, and the current shortage of reef tour capacity is clearly impacting our broader local businesses."

HENRICO COUNTY, Va. — Police used a phone left in a stolen car to track down a driver who drove off in a car that was not his.
The car was left running outside a 7-11 on Williamsburg Road around 8 p.m. on New Year’s Eve.
“The victim stated he left his vehicle running, unlocked, and with his phone in it while he ran into 7-Eleven,” a Henrico Police spokesman said. “He was surprised to find his vehicle missing when he came out.”
Using the phone left in the car, police tracked the vehicle to an address on N. 23rd Street in Richmond.
“Officers arrived to find Mr. [Dustin Avory] Swan driving the stolen car,” police said. “During the arrest, Mr. Swan kicked one of the Henrico officers. Once in custody it was determined that Swan was also intoxicated.”
Swan, 44, was charged with Grand Larceny, Disorderly Conduct, and his second DWI in the last five – 10 years.

Upon returning, he discovered the vehicle was gone.

Authorities tracked the phone to an address on North 23rd Street in Richmond. There, officers found 44-year-old Dustin Avory Swan behind the wheel of the stolen car. During his arrest, Swan allegedly kicked a Henrico police officer. Once in custody, he was also found to be intoxicated. Swan now faces charges including Grand Larceny, Disorderly Conduct, and his second DWI offense within the past five to ten years.

Scientists ID Tiny Prehistoric Sea Worm with 50 Head Spines
Long before dinosaurs roamed the Earth, a bizarre creature with a Venus flytrap-like head swam the seas. Scientists have uncovered fossils of a tiny faceless prehistoric sea worm with 50 spines jutting out of its head. When some unsuspecting critter came too close, its jaw-like spines snapped together and dinner was served.
The discovery reported in Thursday's journal Current Biology offers a glimpse into the Cambrian explosion of life on Earth about 541 million years ago.
The new creature dubbed Capinatator praetermissus is so different that scientists said the fossils represent not only a new species, but a new genus -- a larger grouping of life -- as well.
It was only 4 inches long and its spines were about one-third of an inch long. It feasted on smaller plankton and shrimp-like creatures.
It is an ancestor of a group of marine arrow worms called chaetognatha that are abundant in the world's oceans. The prehistoric version was larger and with far more spines in its facial armory but without the specialized teeth of its descendants, said Derek Briggs of Yale University who led a team that discovered the trove of fossils in two national parks in British Columbia, Canada.
"The spines are like miniature hooks, although more gently curved. They were stiff rather than flexible," Briggs said in an email. "It's hard to say why there are so many spines in the fossil example -- but presumably thus armed it was a successful predator."
Capinatator -- whose name translates to grasping swimmer -- lived 500 million years ago at a time when creatures started getting bigger and more diverse. It's difficult to find complete fossils belonging to the chaetognatha family because they decayed easily, said Briggs. This latest find, however, was so good that even soft tissue was saved, giving scientists a good idea about what Capinatator looked like.
The discovery expands scientists' knowledge of a "pretty enigmatic" group of animals from the Cambrian era, said Smithsonian paleobiologist Doug Erwin, who had no role in the research.

rewrite:
Long before dinosaurs walked the Earth, a strange creature with a head resembling a Venus flytrap swam through ancient seas. Scientists have identified fossils of a small, faceless prehistoric sea worm equipped with 50 spines radiating from its head. When an unsuspecting animal drifted too close, these jaw-like spines would snap shut, capturing its meal.

This discovery, detailed in the journal *Current Biology*, provides a window into the Cambrian explosion, a period roughly 541 million years ago when life on Earth rapidly diversified. The newfound creature, named *Capinatator praetermissus*, is so distinct that researchers say it represents not just a new species, but an entirely new genus—a broader category of life.

Measuring about four inches long, with spines roughly a third of an inch in length, it likely fed on small plankton and shrimp-like organisms. *Capinatator* is an ancient ancestor of modern arrow worms, or chaetognaths, which are plentiful in today’s oceans. According to Derek Briggs of Yale University, who led the team that uncovered the fossils in two Canadian national parks in British Columbia, this prehistoric version was larger and bore significantly more head spines than its descendants, though it lacked their specialized teeth.

“The spines are like miniature hooks, though more gently curved. They were stiff rather than flexible,” Briggs explained via email. “It’s hard to say why there are so many spines in the fossil specimen, but being armed in this way presumably made it a successful predator.”

Living about 500 million years ago, *Capinatator*—whose name means “grasping swimmer”—existed during a time when ocean creatures were growing in size and variety. Briggs notes that complete fossils from the chaetognath family are rare because their bodies decayed easily. This particular find, however, is exceptionally well-preserved, even retaining soft tissues, which gives scientists a clear picture of the animal’s appearance.

The find enhances understanding of what Smithsonian paleobiologist Doug Erwin calls a “pretty enigmatic” group of Cambrian-era animals. Erwin was not involved in the research but acknowledges the significance of the discovery in filling gaps in the early history of marine life.

OTTAWA — Only weeks after Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said Canada was prepared to offer helicopters, aircraft and hundreds of troops to peacekeeping, the number of Canadians on UN missions reached a new low, new figures indicate.
Canada had a total of 43 peacekeepers deployed around the world at the end of December, according to the most recent UN numbers, down from 62 in November.
The decline, largely the result of a reduction in the number of Canadian police officers deployed to Haiti, means Canada has fewer peacekeepers in the field than at any point since the 1950s.
That's despite the Liberals having repeatedly promised to ramp up Canada's contributions to UN missions — most recently by pledging equipment, troops and trainers at a peacekeeping summit that Canada hosted in November.
Canadian and UN officials say the two sides are working to identify when and where those pledges will be utilized, but they have declined to provide any timeline for when a decision will come.
Walter Dorn, an expert on peacekeeping at the Canadian Forces College in Toronto who has been tracking the numbers, said the current situation is shameful given the Trudeau government's repeated promises.
"Canada is at its lowest level since Lester B. Pearson proposed the first peacekeeping force in 1956," Dorn said. "This is hypocrisy, coming after the promises and lofty rhetoric of the Vancouver ministerial."
The Liberals promised during the last federal election to renew Canada's commitment to peacekeeping, and pledged in August 2016 to make up to 600 troops and 150 police officers available for future missions.
Canada had 112 peacekeepers in the field at the time of that promise.
Trudeau announced in Vancouver in November that Canada was offering helicopters, a transport aircraft and a 200-member rapid reaction force for use on UN missions, as well as trainers to help other countries with peacekeeping.

OTTAWA — New figures reveal that the number of Canadian peacekeepers deployed on United Nations missions has hit a record low, coming just weeks after Prime Minister Justin Trudeau pledged helicopters, aircraft, and hundreds of troops to support such operations.

According to the latest UN data, Canada had only 43 peacekeepers stationed worldwide at the end of December, down from 62 in November. This drop—primarily due to fewer Canadian police officers serving in Haiti—marks the country’s smallest peacekeeping presence since the 1950s.

The decline stands in stark contrast to repeated promises from the Liberal government to strengthen Canada’s role in UN missions. Most recently, at a peacekeeping summit hosted by Canada in November, the government committed to providing equipment, troops, and trainers.

Canadian and UN officials say they are collaborating to determine when and where these contributions will be deployed, though no timeline for a decision has been provided.

Walter Dorn, a peacekeeping expert at the Canadian Forces College in Toronto who monitors these figures, called the current situation “shameful” in light of the government’s assurances. “Canada is at its lowest level since Lester B. Pearson proposed the first peacekeeping force in 1956,” Dorn said. “This is hypocrisy, coming after the promises and lofty rhetoric of the Vancouver ministerial.”

During the last federal election, the Liberals vowed to renew Canada’s commitment to peacekeeping, and in August 2016 they pledged to make as many as 600 troops and 150 police officers available for future missions. At the time of that promise, Canada had 112 peacekeepers deployed.

Then, at the Vancouver summit in November, Trudeau announced an offer of helicopters, a transport aircraft, a 200-member rapid reaction force, and additional trainers to assist other nations with peacekeeping—a commitment that has yet to translate into increased personnel on the ground.

JOHNSON CITY, TN (WJHL) – While Wellmont Health System added employees in 2016 compared to 2015, Mountain States Health Alliance reduced its total number of employees by 5%, the equivalent of 470 positions, according to recent tax filings.
A MSHA spokesperson says at the end of 2016, the system employed 8,150 people, which is compared to the 8,620 employees listed on the organization’s most recent tax filing at the end of 2015.
MSHA Chief Financial Officer Lynn Krutak says the organization hasn’t had any reductions in force, but has eliminated non-essential positions, mainly through attrition. Krutak says as the health system is faced with declining reimbursements, management is focused on running a lean organization and eliminating any unnecessary expenses.
“We haven’t reduced any clinical staff,” she said. “We’ve reduced some of the overhead staff, again as we continue to look at every area where we might be able to reduce expenses. There have been some people, but it’s mainly the result of attrition. We haven’t had any reduction in force. We do that through turnover.”
A spokesperson says MSHA has hired 760 people so far this year and currently has 426 open job postings, some of which include multiple positions. MSHA did not release a year-to-date number of employees.
Wellmont reports it employed 6,254 employees at the end of 2016, which was up from 6,106 the year before, according to recent tax filings.

When the Waldport City Council meets next Thursday, there will be lots to talk about, not the least of which will be the applicants to fill a council vacancy. On the list of applicants is a well known figure in local government, the former Port Director of the Port of Newport, Kevin Greenwood. Greenwood applied to fill an unfinished term on the council stating that he has a lot of experience in government work, is active with Waldport Middle School and Crestview Heights Grade School where he has his children enrolled. He also states on his application that he’s active in the Waldport Jr. League.
Also applying for the city council position is Harry Dennis Junior, who sports a college degree in Management and Finance. Mr. Dennis says he has considerable experience in government work from the public works side of things. He’s also the Secretary-Treasurer for the Alsea-Highlands homeowners association. Also applying is Jerry Phillips who is retired from Southern California. Currently he is a member of the Alsea Highlands homeowners association.
Also on next week’s Waldport City Council agenda is an update on a housing development at the south end of SW Norwood – 34 new homes proposed to be going in there by Tidewater Development, LLC.
Long time contract land use planner Dustin Kittel is leaving the city, to be replaced by the former City Manager of Yachats, Joan Davies.
City Manager Kerry Kemp is expected to brief the council on the prospects of a new South County Swim Center proposed by community boosters. Paying for it would be depending on whether the voters would float a higher property tax rate to float bonds to build it. Possible locations include the Commons Ballfields or Angell Job Corps site. Kemp’s report to the council indicates that despite strong community support for the new swim center, it’s likely to be at least five years off, if not a little longer.
The Waldport City Council convenes their meeting October 12th, 2pm at City Hall, behind the fire station off Hemlock.

Among those seeking the position is a familiar name in local governance: Kevin Greenwood, former Port Director of the Port of Newport. In his application, Greenwood cites extensive experience in government work, along with his active involvement in Waldport Middle School and Crestview Heights Grade School, where his children are enrolled. He also notes his participation in the Waldport Jr. League.

Another applicant is Harry Dennis Junior, who holds a college degree in Management and Finance. Mr. Dennis points to considerable experience from the public works side of government and currently serves as Secretary-Treasurer for the Alsea-Highlands homeowners association. Also in the running is Jerry Phillips, a retiree from Southern California who is now a member of the same homeowners association.

In staffing news, long-time contract land use planner Dustin Kittel is departing the city. He will be replaced by Joan Davies, former City Manager of Yachats.

Additionally, City Manager Kerry Kemp is expected to brief the council on the prospects for a new South County Swim Center, an initiative pushed by community boosters. According to Kemp’s report, despite strong community backing, the project is likely at least five years away from becoming a reality.

The Waldport City Council meeting is scheduled for October 12th at 2 p.m. in City Hall, located behind the fire station off Hemlock Street.

While some of Hugh Hefner's Playboy Bunnies may have appeared to be merely scantily clad waitresses, many of these women pursued impressive careers long after leaving the late publisher's lounges. Their stories reveal a depth that goes far beyond the iconic costumes.

Fads and music scenes have come and gone since the 1970s, but Blondie remains one of New York City's best rock 'n' roll bands, kicking as much ass as ever. The punk legends, who released their first album in 1976, are a band constantly changing, much like the city that spawned them. Starting as a throwback act incorporating a ’60s girl-group sound, their evolution is a testament to their enduring relevance. Now, frontwoman Debbie Harry is aiming for the White House's ear, joining an industry-wide chorus—with major labels at her back—in the fight against YouTube, arguing the platform undermines artists' rights.

In other news, pioneering Italian producer Giorgio Moroder, whose juddering synths and disco beats defined the ’70s and ’80s, is back in the public eye. His music, famously claimed to have made "more than a million babies," continues to resonate. Meanwhile, the music world was reminded that Michael Jackson released only six full albums in his last thirty years, an emphasis on quality control that makes the posthumous release of "Xscape" particularly contentious.

In a more somber note, Philip Seymour Hoffman’s accused drug dealer has received unexpected support from Blondie musicians, including Debbie Harry, in his bid for rehabilitation instead of jail time. These interconnected stories from the worlds of music and celebrity highlight lasting legacies, ongoing battles, and the complex paths these figures have taken.

NEW YORK (AP) — The following are the latest developments in financial markets (all times local):

**9:50 a.m.**
The yield on the 10-year Treasury note, a key benchmark for interest rates including mortgages, reached 3 percent in early trading Tuesday for the first time since January 2014. The move reflects growing market expectations for stronger inflation and economic growth. The yield later slipped back to 2.99 percent.

Stocks moved broadly higher in early trading, buoyed by a series of solid corporate earnings reports that encouraged investor buying. Notable gainers included Verizon, Harley-Davidson, and Fifth Third Bancorp. The S&P 500 index rose 3 points, or 0.2 percent, to 2,674. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 47 points, or 0.2 percent, to 24,523, while the Nasdaq increased 11 points, or 0.2 percent, to 7,139. Bond prices declined.

**9:35 a.m.**
Stocks opened broadly higher on Wall Street as robust earnings reports from several companies spurred investor optimism. Verizon, Harley-Davidson, and Fifth Third Bancorp all rose sharply after posting results that exceeded analysts' forecasts. Google's parent company, Alphabet, also reported surging earnings, but its stock fell 2.2 percent as the company noted a sharp increase in spending. In other corporate news, drugmaker Shire gained 3.3 percent after announcing it had received a new takeover offer from Japanese rival Takeda.

In early trading, the S&P 500 index rose 9 points, or 0.4 percent, to 2,680. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 71 points, or 0.3 percent, to 24,523, and the Nasdaq increased 34 points, or 0.5 percent, to 7,162. Bond prices fell, pushing the yield on the 10-year Treasury note to 2.99 percent.

NEW YORK With the U.S. economy having now "largely attained" a full recovery from recession, the Federal Reserve can raise interest rates three or more times this year, a centrist Fed policymaker said on Wednesday.
San Francisco Fed President John Williams, who largely repeated his view that the U.S. central bank should continue tightening policy gradually, said the main obstacles to raising economic output are now largely outside of the Fed's realm of influence: the slow growth in new workers in the labor market and in their productivity on the job.
He said such supply-side impediments to pushing overall economic growth above its current 2-percent rate are for lawmakers and business leaders to tackle, not the Federal Reserve.
Lifting rates gradually "prevents the economy from overheating... I would not rule out more than three increases total for this year," Williams told an economists' club in New York.
"With an economy at full employment, inflation nearing the Fed's 2 percent goal, and the expansion now in its eighth year, the data have spoken and the message is clear: We've largely attained the hard-sought recovery we've been after for the past nine years," added Williams, who is close to Fed Chair Janet Yellen and who regains a vote on the Fed's policy committee next year under a rotation.
Earlier this month the Fed lifted rates a notch, its third tightening since the 2007-2009 financial crisis and recession. Forecasts from Fed officials suggest a median of two more hikes are planned before year end.
Williams expects economic growth of around 1.75 percent this year and next, a bit below his colleagues, and for inflation to hit 2 percent in the next year or so.
(Reporting by Jonathan Spicer; Editing by Chizu Nomiyama)
rewrite:
NEW YORK—With the U.S. economy having now “largely achieved” a full recovery from recession, the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates three or more times this year, a centrist Fed policymaker said Wednesday.

San Francisco Fed President John Williams reiterated his view that the U.S. central bank should continue tightening monetary policy gradually. He noted that the main constraints on boosting economic output now lie largely outside the Fed’s control—namely, slow growth in the labor force and weak gains in productivity.

Such supply-side limits, which are holding overall economic growth near its current 2 percent pace, must be addressed by lawmakers and business leaders rather than the Fed, Williams said.

A gradual pace of rate increases “prevents the economy from overheating … I would not rule out more than three increases total for this year,” he told an economists’ group in New York.

“With an economy at full employment, inflation nearing the Fed’s 2 percent goal, and the expansion now in its eighth year, the data have spoken and the message is clear: We’ve largely attained the hard‑sought recovery we’ve been after for the past nine years,” added Williams. He is viewed as aligned with Fed Chair Janet Yellen and will regain a vote on the policy committee next year under a rotation system.

Earlier this month, the Fed raised rates modestly—its third hike since the 2007‑2009 financial crisis and recession. Forecasts from Fed officials point to a median expectation of two additional increases before year‑end.

Williams expects economic growth of about 1.75 percent this year and next, slightly below the estimates of many of his colleagues, and projects inflation will reach 2 percent in the coming year or so.

BERLIN The European Union should try to limit the fallout from Britain's decision to leave the European Union, German Chancellor Angela Merkel said on Monday, conceding that some damage was inevitable.
"This is an incision for the European Union, it's an unfortunate event - Britain's decision," Merkel told a joint news conference with Slovakian Prime Minister Robert Fico and Czech Prime Minister Bohuslav Sobotka in Berlin.
"We want to limit the damage. But there will naturally be some negative impact," Merkel said, adding that it was more important that the remaining 27 EU member states stick together and improve the competitiveness of the bloc.
(Reporting by Joseph Nasr and Paul Carrel)
rewrite:
On April 3, 2017, German Chancellor Angela Merkel hosted a joint news conference at the Chancellery in Berlin with Slovakian Prime Minister Robert Fico and Czech Prime Minister Bohuslav Sobotka. The three leaders were photographed arriving at and attending the event, where Merkel emphasized the need for a unified European response to Britain's decision to leave the European Union.

Addressing the media, Chancellor Merkel described Brexit as "an incision for the European Union" and "an unfortunate event." She acknowledged that some negative impact was inevitable but stressed that the priority must be to limit the damage. "We want to limit the damage. But there will naturally be some negative impact," Merkel stated. She argued that it was now more important than ever for the remaining 27 member states to maintain solidarity and work together to enhance the bloc's overall competitiveness.

The meeting underscored the collaborative effort among key EU leaders to navigate the political and economic uncertainties following the British referendum. By presenting a united front, Merkel, Fico, and Sobotka aimed to project stability and a shared commitment to the European project during a period of significant transition.

Image copyright Highways England Image caption Six junctions are due for a revamp in the proposals
A consultation into improvements on the A27 has been dubbed "a sham" by council leaders.
Highways England plans to "increase capacity and reduce congestion" between Worthing and Lancing.
But Adur and Worthing councils say the £69m proposal is not fit for purpose and the government body should launch a fresh consultation with updated plans.
Highways England project manager Tom Beasley said the improvements were the "best achievable option".
Large-scale options were considered by Highways England, including dual carriageway schemes with flyovers.
But the consultation focuses a mix of new traffic signalling and road widening on six junctions between Durrington Hill and the Lancing Manor roundabout.
'Best option'
In a joint statement, the leader of Adur District Council, Neil Parkin, and the leader of Worthing Borough Council, Dan Humphreys, said the "modest" plans are not good enough.
Mr Parkin said: "Highways England say they want to consult with us but we say this is a sham. By not allowing the public to weigh up options and see full costings how are we to make any kind of decision?
"All I do know is the current scheme on the table is barely worth the disruption and certainly not worth spending £69m on."
Mr Humphreys added: "Highways England do not seem to be taking us seriously. Our questions were met with an 'experts know best' response."
But Mr Beasley said Highways England think that the proposal "would make a worthwhile improvement to people's journeys and is the best achievable option within the scope and budget available for the project".
"We welcome all views and promise that we will take all responses to the consultation fully into account."
Consultation into the proposal ends on 12 September.
rewrite:
A proposed £69 million upgrade to the A27 between Worthing and Lancing has been labeled “a sham” by local council leaders. Highways England, which aims to increase capacity and reduce congestion on the stretch, is consulting on plans focusing on six junctions from Durrington Hill to Lancing Manor roundabout. The proposals involve a combination of new traffic signals and road widening.

However, the leaders of Adur and Worthing councils have issued a joint statement calling the plans “modest” and unfit for purpose. They argue that the public consultation is flawed because it does not allow for a comparison of different options or a full view of costs. “Highways England say they want to consult with us, but we say this is a sham,” said Adur leader Neil Parkin. “By not allowing the public to weigh up options and see full costings, how are we to make any kind of decision? The current scheme is barely worth the disruption and certainly not worth spending £69 million on.”

Worthing leader Dan Humphreys added, “Highways England do not seem to be taking us seriously. Our questions were met with an ‘experts know best’ response.”

Tom Beasley, the project manager for Highways England, defended the proposal, stating that while larger-scale options like dual carriageways with flyovers were considered, the current plan represents the “best achievable option” within the project’s scope and budget. “We believe it would make a worthwhile improvement to people’s journeys,” he said. “We welcome all views and promise to take all responses to the consultation fully into account.”

The consultation on the proposed improvements is set to close on September 12.

Doctor-assisted suicide in Canada consists of a lethal injection in hospital or at home (AFP Photo/PATRICK KOVARIK)
Ottawa (AFP) - Nearly 2,000 people with incurable diseases were helped to die by a doctor in the first year since Canada legalized medically-assisted suicide, according to a report published Friday.
From the time Ottawa passed the legislation in June 2016 to June 30, 2017, 1,982 people ended their lives in this way, according to Health Canada.
Most had cancer, the agency said.
Extrapolating from the data collected for the first half of 2017, the number of assisted deaths is expected to rise but remain at less than two percent of all deaths nationwide this year -- "consistent with international experience," it said a statement.
Doctor-assisted suicide in Canada is reserved for adults with serious health problems who want to end their suffering, and consists of a lethal injection in hospital or at home.
Days after the law was changed to allow for the practice, it was challenged in court in an attempt to expand it to include Canadians who suffer from a wasting disease but who are not facing imminent death.
These include people suffering from spinal muscular atrophy, multiple sclerosis, spinal stenosis, locked in syndrome, traumatic spinal injury, Parkinson's disease and Huntington's disease.
Canadian bishops have instructed their clergy to deny religious funerals for deceased persons who chose a doctor-assisted suicide.
rewrite:
In Canada, doctor-assisted suicide involves a lethal injection administered either in a hospital or at home, as reported by AFP. According to figures released on Friday, nearly 2,000 individuals with incurable conditions opted for medically assisted death in the first year following its legalization. Health Canada’s data, covering June 2016 through June 2017, shows that 1,982 people ended their lives through this process, with cancer being the most common underlying illness.

Based on projections from early 2017, the annual number of assisted deaths is anticipated to increase, though it will likely remain below two percent of all deaths nationwide—a pattern consistent with international trends. Under Canadian law, this option is available only to adults experiencing severe and enduring suffering due to a grievous medical condition.

Shortly after the legislation took effect, a court challenge sought to broaden its scope to include patients with degenerative illnesses, such as multiple sclerosis or Parkinson’s disease, who are not necessarily near death. Meanwhile, Canada’s Catholic bishops have directed clergy to refuse religious funeral rites to those who choose medically assisted dying.

A 68-year-old man who suffered a heart attack at a leisure centre has praised quick-thinking staff and paramedics for saving his life.
Alan Hartley, of Elmswell, was on a treadmill at Everyone Active Leisure Centre, in Stowmarket, on January 23 when he collapsed and went into cardiac arrest.
Gym staff rushed to his rescue with a defibrillator and, together with the East of England Ambulance Service NHS Trust (EEAST), helped revive him. Now recovering well, he reunited with his life-savers on Monday to thank them.
He said: “The gym staff don’t go to work and expect to save a life and for that I owe them so much. It’s amazing to be able to thank them in person.”
When he collapsed, Becky Cruikshank, from Everyone Active, shouted for help, pushed a panic button and, when it became clear Mr Hartley wasn’t breathing, she started chest compressions.
Her colleague Steve Ward brought the gym’s defibrillator and administered the first and most vital shock.
He said: “You just go into auto pilot in those situations. I just saw someone who was very sick and needed our help.”
Medics from the EEAST were dispatched and the air ambulance called.
The ambulance crew shocked him a further two times and resuscitated him.
Mr Hartley was flown to Norfolk and Norwich University Hospital where he remained for three days before being discharged.
He had suffered a total blockage of his anterior lateral artery.
Gym staff have received certificates of thanks from the EEAST.
Paramedic supervisor James Mullett said: “The quick recognition of the severity of the incident by the gym staff as well as early cardio pulmonary resuscitation and the use of a defibrillator ensured Alan had the best chance of survival.”
He added: “I would also like to thank the call handler and dispatcher involved; they deserve credit for delivering excellent instructions over the phone as well as dispatching the appropriate resources Alan needed. Everyone did their part to give Alan his life back to him.”
For more information on how defibrillators work, watch this short video at www.youtube.com
Anyone who is interested in working for the ambulance service should visit www.eastamb.nhs.uk

A 68-year-old man whose life was saved after he suffered a heart attack at his local leisure centre has praised the quick-thinking staff and paramedics who came to his aid. Alan Hartley, from Elmswell, was using a treadmill at the Everyone Active Leisure Centre in Stowmarket on January 23 when he collapsed and went into cardiac arrest.

Gym employees immediately rushed to his side with a defibrillator and, working alongside the East of England Ambulance Service NHS Trust (EEAST), helped revive him. Now recovering well, Mr. Hartley reunited with his rescuers on Monday to express his gratitude. “The gym staff don’t come to work expecting to save a life—and for that I owe them so much,” he said. “It’s amazing to be able to thank them in person.”

When Mr. Hartley collapsed, Becky Cruikshank, a staff member at Everyone Active, called for help, activated a panic button, and—realizing he was not breathing—began chest compressions. Her colleague, Steve Ward, brought over the gym’s defibrillator and delivered the first, crucial shock. Reflecting on the incident, Mr. Ward said, “You just go into autopilot in those situations. I saw someone who was very sick and needed our help.”

Medics from EEAST were promptly dispatched, and the air ambulance was called. The ambulance crew administered two further shocks and successfully resuscitated Mr. Hartley. He was then flown to Norfolk and Norwich University Hospital, where he remained for three days before being discharged. Doctors confirmed he had suffered a complete blockage of his anterior lateral artery.

In recognition of their actions, the gym staff have received certificates of thanks from EEAST. Paramedic supervisor James Mullett commented, “The gym staff’s quick recognition of the severity of the incident, along with early CPR and the use of a defibrillator, ensured Alan had the best possible chance of survival.” He added, “I would also like to thank the call handler and dispatcher involved. They deserve credit for providing excellent instructions over the phone and deploying the resources Alan needed. Everyone played their part in giving Alan his life back.”

For more information on how defibrillators work, you can watch a short video at www.youtube.com. Anyone interested in working for the ambulance service is encouraged to visit www.eastamb.nhs.uk.

HOUSTON (AP) — Texans coach Bill O'Brien says he wouldn't have let Tom Savage re-enter Sunday's game after an alarming hit that gave him a concussion and left the quarterback's hands shaking if he had seen the video of the hit.
Savage was injured with about nine minutes remaining in the second quarter of Houston's 26-16 loss to San Francisco when he was driven to the ground on a hit by Elvis Dumervil.
Replays showed Savage looking dazed after his head hit the ground with both of his arms shaking and lifted upward.
He was taken to the medical tent where he stayed for less than three minutes before returning to the bench and going back in for the next series.
Savage threw two incompletions on that drive, and Houston's team doctor approached him after he returned to the sideline at the end of that possession.
He was then evaluated again and taken to the locker room after it was determined that he did have a concussion.
On Monday O'Brien said: "There's no video on the sideline. All there are are tablets. There's no video, there's nothing like that. With benefit of seeing the video ... (and) the care for the player, I would've never let that player back in the game, and I don't believe that (trainer) Geoff Kaplan would've allowed that player back in the game. I don't have benefit of the video. I did not see anything."
Also on Monday an NFL spokesman said the league is looking into whether concussion protocol was properly followed after Savage was injured.
League spokesman Joe Lockhart said the NFL and the players' association "together will conduct a thorough review of the incident focused on whether the protocol was properly followed, but we're also continuing looking at the protocol to look for ways to improve and strengthen it."
___
AP Pro Football Writer Barry Wilner contributed to this report.
___

HOUSTON (AP) — Houston Texans coach Bill O’Brien stated Monday that he would not have allowed quarterback Tom Savage to return to Sunday’s game after a hard hit left him concussed and visibly shaken—if he had seen video of the incident at the time.

Savage was injured with roughly nine minutes left in the second quarter of Houston’s 26–16 loss to the San Francisco 49ers. He was driven to the ground on a hit by Elvis Dumervil, and replays showed him appearing dazed after his head struck the turf, with both arms trembling and lifted upward.

After being examined in the medical tent for less than three minutes, Savage returned to the sideline and re-entered the game for the next series. He threw two incomplete passes on that drive, and the team’s doctor approached him once he came back to the sideline. Savage was then reevaluated, diagnosed with a concussion, and taken to the locker room.

O’Brien explained Monday, “There’s no video on the sideline. All there are are tablets. There’s no video, there’s nothing like that. With the benefit of seeing the video … and out of care for the player, I would’ve never let that player back in the game, and I don’t believe that trainer Geoff Kaplan would’ve allowed that player back in the game. I don’t have benefit of the video. I did not see anything.”

Also on Monday, an NFL spokesman said the league is reviewing whether concussion protocol was properly followed after Savage’s injury. League spokesman Joe Lockhart noted that the NFL and the players’ association “together will conduct a thorough review of the incident focused on whether the protocol was properly followed, but we’re also continuing to look at the protocol to find ways to improve and strengthen it.”

___

AP Pro Football Writer Barry Wilner contributed to this report.

Willie Walsh, chief executive of Aer Lingus parent, International Airlines Group (IAG), says the business is happy with the response to its new budget carrier, Level.
IAG launched the new Barcelona-based airline in March and it plans to begin flying to LA, San Francisco, Buenos Aires in Argentine and Punta Cana in the Dominican Republic from June.
The move is designed to combat the launch of cheap transatlantic services by the likes of Norwegian, which will begin services from Ireland to the US in July, and Wow, which offers flights from the Europe to north America via Rekjavik.
Mr Walsh said over the weekend that bookings on its site, flylevel, are strong, with more than 50 per cent of customers in the key 18 to 34 years age bracket. “So it´s an interesting demographic,” he told CNN´s Quest Means Business.
Speaking to the same programme, commentator Ben Schlappig, editor of travel blog, One Mile at a Time, said that it was a case of “monkey see, monkey do”.
He argued that the threat posed by Norwegian and Wow was such that British Airways – one of IAG´s other three airlines – had “no choice” but to follow with a low-cost carrier of its own.
He noted that there were suggestions that British Airways could introduce paid-for meals on its transatlantic economy flights in much the same as Norwegian is already doing.
Shortly after Norwegian announced details of its Irish services, Aer Lingus chief executive, Stephen Kavanagh, indicated that the airline could introduce cheaper no-frills fares on its transatlantic flights, that would exclude elements normally found in ticket prices.
rewrite:
Willie Walsh, the chief executive of International Airlines Group (IAG), which owns Aer Lingus, has expressed satisfaction with the early reception for its new low-cost airline, Level. Launched in March from Barcelona, Level is scheduled to commence flights in June to destinations including Los Angeles, San Francisco, Buenos Aires, and Punta Cana. This initiative is a strategic response to the expansion of budget transatlantic services by carriers such as Norwegian, which will begin U.S. flights from Ireland in July, and Wow Air, which connects Europe and North America via Reykjavik.

Mr. Walsh noted over the weekend that bookings on Level's website are robust, with more than half of its customers falling within the key 18 to 34 age demographic. "So it's an interesting demographic," he remarked in an interview with CNN's Quest Means Business. Appearing on the same program, travel commentator Ben Schlappig, editor of the blog One Mile at a Time, described the move as a classic case of "monkey see, monkey do." He contended that the competitive threat from Norwegian and Wow Air left British Airways—another IAG subsidiary—with "no choice" but to develop its own low-cost offering.

Schlappig also observed that there is speculation British Airways might begin charging for meals on its transatlantic economy flights, similar to Norwegian's model. In a related development, shortly after Norwegian detailed its Irish-based services, Aer Lingus CEO Stephen Kavanagh suggested his airline might introduce simpler, cheaper fares for transatlantic routes, stripping out amenities typically included in the ticket price.

Way back in March, Klay Thompson signed a fan’s Warriors-themed toaster at an event. Thompson looked so incredibly confused while signing it that the photo went viral.
Then, after that toaster was signed, the Warriors went on an amazing win streak. They only lost two games from March 14 (the day after Thompson held the toaster) through Game 5 of the Finals, and now they’re the champs. Was it because of the power of the toaster?
Thompson was even commenting on the toaster throughout the playoffs, and apparently he still has it on his mind because the owner of the all-powerful toaster says that Thompson invited him to the team’s championship parade.

As noted, Illinois tattoo artist Catherine Alexander recently filed a lawsuit against WWE and 2K Games over the use of Randy Orton's tattoos in the WWE 2K video game series. Alexander, who has done Orton's ink since 2003, claims she owns the copyrights to the designs. She has accused WWE and 2K of copyright infringement because Orton's tats are depicted to a tee in the games. TMZ Sports noted that Alexander claims she brought the issue up with WWE in 2009 and was offered just $450 for the rights to use the designs, which she declined.
The suit was filed on April 17th in the United States District Court of Southern District of Illinois and also names 2K Sports, Take-Two Interactive Software, Visual Concepts Entertainment, Yuke's Co. and Yuke's LA as defendants. PWInsider adds that Alexander has requested a jury trial and is asking the court to rule that the tattoos are her copyrighted works, and that the defendants infringed against her. She is also asking the court to rule that she is owed damages but there's no word yet on how much she's seeking. None of the defendants have responded to the lawsuit as of this week.
Alexander's suit claims that all of her tattoos on Orton are her original designs and that she never gave the defendants permission to recreate them in WWE video games. Alexander says she did the work on Orton between 2003 and 2008, and that the tattoos are "easily recognized by his fans and members of the public."
Alexander submitted applications to register copyrights on each tattoo on March 15th of this year.
The suit also says Orton does not have ownership of the copyrights and has no authority to, and did not grant permission to, the defendants. It should be noted that Orton is not listed as a defendant.
rewrite:
Illinois tattoo artist Catherine Alexander, known for her long-standing work with WWE star Randy Orton, has filed a lawsuit against WWE and 2K Games. The legal action centers on the unauthorized reproduction of Orton’s tattoos in the WWE 2K video game series. Alexander, who has been Orton’s tattoo artist since 2003, asserts that she holds the copyrights to the original designs. She alleges that WWE and 2K committed copyright infringement by replicating the tattoos in precise detail across multiple game installments. According to TMZ Sports, Alexander raised the issue with WWE as early as 2009, at which time she was offered a mere $450 for the rights to use the designs—an offer she refused.

The lawsuit was officially filed on April 17th in the United States District Court for the Southern District of Illinois. In addition to WWE and 2K Games, the defendants include 2K Sports, Take-Two Interactive Software, Visual Concepts Entertainment, Yuke’s Co., and Yuke’s LA. As reported by PWInsider, Alexander has requested a jury trial. She is seeking a court declaration that the tattoos are her copyrighted works and that the defendants infringed upon them. The filing also asks the court to award her damages, though the specific amount has not yet been disclosed. None of the named defendants had responded to the suit as of this week.

Alexander’s complaint emphasizes that all tattoos she applied to Orton between 2003 and 2008 are her original artistic creations, and she never granted permission for their reproduction in video games. She notes that these designs are widely recognized by Orton’s fans and the general public. To strengthen her claim, Alexander submitted applications to register copyrights for each individual tattoo on March 15th of this year.

The suit further clarifies that Orton himself does not own the copyrights to the tattoos, nor did he have the authority to grant permission for their use. It is worth noting that Orton is not named as a defendant in the case.

By Sarah Stockman
Staff Writer
One sunny morning in February I sat in my kitchen waiting for the doorbell to ring. Any minute Palisadian Reed Newman would arrive to tell me about his vegetable garden growing company Revival Roots.
Normally when I interview someone we meet at a neutral location like Starbucks. However, I had taken Newman up on his offer on NextDoor for free garden consultations since I was curious how his company worked.
There was potentially one small hiccup: I live with my parents so I had to ask permission to invite him over. Luckily they didn’t have any problems. “Ask him about replacing sprinklers,” my mom told me. “Tell him to bring us some free plants,” my dad added.
And so I found myself waiting one Tuesday morning for Newman’s arrival.
Newman, 24, grew up in West Los Angeles and Santa Monica Canyon with his twin older siblings and his parents Jeanne and Gary, who are in the entertainment industry.
“We grew up in West Los Angeles and moved to Santa Monica Canyon about six years ago,” Newman said.

One sunny February morning, I waited in my kitchen for the doorbell to ring. Palisadian Reed Newman was due to arrive any moment to tell me about his vegetable garden company, Revival Roots. Typically, I conduct interviews in neutral spots like coffee shops, but I had accepted Newman’s offer—posted on NextDoor—for a free garden consultation, eager to see how his business operated.

There was just one small hiccup: I live with my parents, so I needed their permission to invite him over. Fortunately, they agreed without issue. “Ask him about replacing the sprinklers,” my mom suggested. My dad chimed in, “Tell him to bring us some free plants!”

And so, that Tuesday morning, I found myself anticipating Newman’s arrival. Newman, 24, grew up in West Los Angeles and Santa Monica Canyon alongside his twin older siblings and his parents, Jeanne and Gary, who work in the entertainment industry. “We grew up in West L.A.,” he explained, “and moved to Santa Monica Canyon about six years ago.”
