TRIPOLI May 3 Rival Libyan camps issued separate statements on Wednesday promising to calm tensions in southern Libya and fight terrorism, but offering no shared way forward for a political deal to unify the North African country.
The statements came a day after intense diplomatic pressure resulted in a meeting in Abu Dhabi between eastern-based commander Khalifa Haftar and the head of the U.N.-backed government in Tripoli, Fayez Seraj.
Haftar is the key figure for eastern factions that, frustrating international efforts to end Libya's conflict, spurned Seraj's Government of National Accord (GNA) after it was established in the capital last year.
There was no mention in the statement from Seraj of plans reported by pro-Haftar media on Tuesday to restructure the unity government's leadership and hold fresh elections next year.
A source close to the GNA leadership said the two sides had initially tried to agree on a joint statement before deciding to issue separate declarations.
Conflicting accounts of initial agreements and leaks of documents neither side signed have in the past confused international mediation and negotiations to end the conflict in Libya, which fell into factional fighting in the years after a 2011 civil war ousted Muammar Gaddafi. (Reporting by Aidan Lewis in Tunis, Ahmed Elumami in Tripoli and Ayman al-Warfalli in Benghazi; editing by Patrick Markey and John Stonestreet)
rewrite:
On Wednesday, rival factions in Libya each released statements pledging to ease tensions in the country's south and combat terrorism. However, they failed to outline any common path toward a political agreement to unify the nation. These declarations followed a meeting in Abu Dhabi the previous day between Khalifa Haftar, the commander based in eastern Libya, and Fayez Seraj, who heads the U.N.-backed government in Tripoli. That meeting came after significant diplomatic pressure.

Haftar is a central figure for eastern factions that have rejected Seraj's Government of National Accord (GNA), established in Tripoli last year, thereby frustrating international peace efforts. Seraj's statement made no reference to plans, reported the day before by pro-Haftar media, to restructure the unity government's leadership and hold new elections next year.

According to a source close to the GNA leadership, the two sides initially attempted to draft a joint statement before opting to issue separate ones. Past mediation efforts have often been muddled by conflicting versions of preliminary agreements and the leaking of unsigned documents. Libya has been mired in factional conflict since the 2011 civil war that toppled Muammar Gaddafi.

DAYTON, Ohio (WDTN) – Police in Dayton were called to the 2700 block of Wayne Avenue Sunday after a man said he was robbed.
The incident happened around 6:30 pm Sunday when a man was trying to sell a sweatshirt using a popular phone app.
When officers arrived they met with a man who said he was there to meet with a man to sell his “Peace Skateboard” sweatshirt using the app “Let Go”. The victim told police the person he was there to meet identified himself as Glen Smith, who claimed to be 15-years-old and could not drive.
According to a police report on the incident, when the victim arrived at the agreed meeting place, Smith was not there. Through several text messages, the victim agreed to meet Smith in another location.
When the victim arrived at the intersection of Maplewood Avenue and Kathleen Avenue, he met with Glen and a third person. The men talked for about an hour when Smith claimed he had lost his money. The victim then told Glen he had other things to do and had to leave.
According to the report, the man who identified himself as Glen Smith gave the sweatshirt to his masked friend who then ran off. When the victim confronted “Glen” about it Gen pulled a silver, semi-automatic handgun from his waistband and fired one shot into the air.
The victim then ran away and told police he heard a second shot fired.
No arrests have been made in this case.
rewrite:
DAYTON, Ohio (WDTN) – Dayton police responded to a reported robbery Sunday evening in the 2700 block of Wayne Avenue. The incident began around 6:30 p.m. when a man arranged to sell a sweatshirt through a popular phone-based marketplace app.

Upon arrival, officers spoke with the victim, who explained he had planned to meet a buyer to sell his “Peace Skateboard” sweatshirt using the app “LetGo.” The prospective buyer identified himself as Glen Smith, claimed to be 15 years old, and said he could not drive.

According to the police report, the victim went to the initially agreed location, but Smith was not there. After exchanging several text messages, the victim agreed to meet at a different spot—the intersection of Maplewood Avenue and Kathleen Avenue.

There, the victim encountered Smith and another individual. After conversing for roughly an hour, Smith stated he had lost his money. When the victim said he needed to leave, the person claiming to be Glen Smith handed the sweatshirt to his masked companion, who immediately fled with it.

As the victim confronted “Glen” about the theft, the suspect pulled a silver semi-automatic handgun from his waistband and fired one shot into the air. The victim ran from the scene and reported hearing a second gunshot as he escaped.

No arrests have been made, and the investigation is ongoing.

At an OLOST press conference held Monday afternoon at the Macon-Bibb County Government Center, Macon-Bibb County Commissioner Al Tillman addressed the media. Joined by fellow commissioners Elaine Lucas, Larry Schlesinger, and Virgil Watkins, Tillman urged local state leaders to reach an agreement on legislation. A woman walks past a branch of The Co-operative Bank in London, Britain.
London: Britain’s Cooperative Bank, rescued from the brink of collapse by a group of hedge funds in 2013, has put itself up for sale as it seeks to build up its capital to meet regulatory requirements.
The bank said on Monday that it had made considerable progress implementing its turnaround plan, cutting its cost base by a fifth since 2014.
But it still expects to make a “significant loss” for last year and said that building up capital has proved difficult given low interest rates.
“As a result, and having concluded its annual planning review, the board is today commencing a sale process, inviting offers for all of the issued ordinary share capital in the bank,” the bank said.
The Bank of England’s Prudential Regulation Authority, which regulates Cooperative Bank, said it welcomed the measures announced on Monday.
“We will continue to assess the bank’s progress in building greater financial resilience over the coming months,” the PRA said in a statement.
The Cooperative Bank, which has four million customers, said it was also considering ways to raise equity capital from existing and new capital providers, and a potential “liability management exercise” of its outstanding public debt.
Last month, the bank said it expected its core capital ratio to fall below 10 per cent, falling short of regulatory requirements.
The bank’s immediate issue is the repayment of £400 million (Dh1.8 billion) worth of bonds that mature in September.
Co-op Bank nearly folded in 2013 with a £1.5 billion hole in its capital after losses from problem real estate loans.
The bank was rescued by bondholders, including hedge funds, mainly from the United States, who bet that rising interest rates and a cost-cutting turnaround plan would improve the bank’s fortunes and make them a return on their investment.

Rescued from near-collapse in 2013 by a consortium of hedge funds, the British bank has announced it is up for sale as it strives to bolster its capital to satisfy regulatory demands.

On Monday, the bank reported substantial progress in executing its turnaround strategy, having reduced its cost base by a fifth since 2014. Nevertheless, it anticipates posting a “significant loss” for the past year and acknowledged that accumulating capital remains challenging in a persistent low-interest-rate environment. “Consequently, following its annual planning review, the board has decided to initiate a sale process and is inviting offers for all of the bank’s issued ordinary share capital,” the statement read.

The Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) of the Bank of England, which oversees the Co-operative Bank, expressed support for the measures announced. “We will continue to monitor the bank’s progress in strengthening its financial resilience over the coming months,” the PRA noted in a release.

With four million customers, the bank added that it is exploring options to raise equity capital from both current and new investors, alongside a possible “liability management exercise” to address its outstanding public debt. This comes after the bank warned last month that its core capital ratio is likely to dip below 10 percent, failing to meet regulatory thresholds. Its survival was secured by bondholders—primarily U.S.-based hedge funds—who wagered that rising interest rates and a stringent cost-cutting overhaul would revive the bank’s prospects and yield returns on their investment.

There’s all kinds of threats flying around these days — North Korea threatening Guam, China threatening to cut off trade to North Korea, and Donald Trump threatening pretty much everyone. Now you can add a new ultimatum to the list, this one from Nicolás Maduro Guerra, the son of the Venezuelan president. He didn’t take kindly to Trump’s pronouncement that he would use military force in Venezuela if necessary, and now Guerra says not only would he retaliate if that came to pass, that retaliation would come in the form of actually taking the White House by force.
“If the unlikely event of defiling the homeland came to pass, the rifles would arrive in New York, ” Guerra announced to Venezuelan state media. “Mr. Trump, we would arrive and take the White House.”
Ignoring for a moment that the White House is not in New York, this is Guerra’s comeback to Trump’s recent comment that “Venezuela is not very far away and the people are suffering, and they are dying. We have many options for Venezuela, including a possible military option if necessary.”
That was a response after Maduro’s recent dismissal of Venezuelan parliament and replacement with his own Constituent Assembly. At least for now, Venezuela’s military is busy keeping the peace in Caracas, where protests have broken out amongst Venezuelans tired of food shortages, worthless currency, the not-so-mysterious disappearance of their fellow citizens, and general chaos.
Guerra isn’t the only Venezuelan to respond to Trump’s threat, though. Venezuelan Defense Minister Vladimir Padrino said it would be a “crazy act” if Trump actually tried it. Not that it would it be the first time the U.S. involved itself in Venezuela’s political woes or the governments of Latin American nations. None of those contras have yet resulted in Venezuelans storming the White House, but as always, these are complicated situations with one very uncomplicated U.S. president in charge.
(Via CNN)
rewrite:
Threats seem to be flying from all directions lately—North Korea menacing Guam, China warning it could cut off trade with North Korea, and Donald Trump leveling warnings at nearly everyone. Now, a new ultimatum has entered the fray, this time from Nicolás Maduro Guerra, the son of Venezuela’s president. He did not take kindly to Trump’s recent statement that he would consider using military force in Venezuela if necessary. Guerra has now declared that, should such an intervention occur, he would not only retaliate—he would do so by seizing the White House itself.

“If the unlikely event of defiling the homeland came to pass, the rifles would arrive in New York,” Guerra told Venezuelan state media. “Mr. Trump, we would arrive and take the White House.” Setting aside the geographical error—the White House is not, in fact, in New York—this was his direct response to Trump’s earlier remarks. The U.S. president had stated, “Venezuela is not very far away and the people are suffering, and they are dying. We have many options for Venezuela, including a possible military option if necessary.”

Trump’s comments came after Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro recently dismissed the national parliament and replaced it with a loyalist Constituent Assembly. For now, Venezuela’s military remains occupied maintaining order in Caracas, where protests have erupted amid widespread frustration over severe food shortages, a collapsed currency, unexplained disappearances of citizens, and general turmoil.

Guerra is not alone in pushing back against Trump’s threat. Venezuelan Defense Minister Vladimir Padrino called any potential U.S. military action a “crazy act.” It would not, however, be the first time the United States involved itself in Venezuela’s political struggles—or in the affairs of Latin American governments more broadly. While none of those past interventions have led to Venezuelans storming the White House, the situation remains complex, complicated further by a U.S. president known for his blunt approach.

Shaner Elementary in Topeka is one of three elementary schools ceasing elementary operations after this year, and the students there are planning to give it a proper sendoff.
“At Shaner, we’re going to be holding a very special community publishing party,” said Communities in School coordinator Susan Ortega. “This is an opportunity for our students to sort of write a good-bye letter to Shaner, letting us know what their best memories and good times were, as well as if they have something they want to say to the building one last time before they head on to Jardine Academy.
The publishing party event is this coming Sunday, April 23rd from 2 p.m. to 4 p.m. at the school.
“We want our community members, either former students or former staff members to come back in and really have a chance to share their memories, as well,” said Ortega. “At 2:30 on the day of our celebration, we’re going to be recognizing all the former teachers and staff members.”
The Shaner group has been close knit from the beginning.
“We’re talking about a student population that’s been less than 190 students,” said Ortega. “When you consider some of the sizes of the other elementary schools in Topeka, that’s actually a pretty small school. We only have 11 total classes in our entire building. Getting to have that sort of intimate contact with students where you get to see them on a daily basis and you learn every person’s name, it’s been amazing.”
Shaner, Bishop and Avondale West elementary students will combine to form Jardine Academy beginning this fall.
rewrite:
Shaner Elementary in Topeka is one of three elementary schools that will close its doors after this school year, and the community is preparing a heartfelt farewell. To mark the occasion, students are organizing a special event to honor their school’s legacy.

“We’re holding a very special community publishing party at Shaner,” said Susan Ortega, coordinator for Communities in Schools. “This gives our students a chance to write a kind of goodbye letter to the school—sharing their favorite memories and good times, or anything they might want to say to the building one last time before moving on to Jardine Academy.”

The publishing party is scheduled for Sunday, April 23, from 2 p.m. to 4 p.m. at the school. Ortega added, “We also welcome former students and staff to come back and share their memories. At 2:30 during the celebration, we’ll take time to recognize all the former teachers and staff members.”

Shaner has long been known for its close-knit community. “Our student population has always been under 190,” Ortega noted. “Compared to other elementary schools in Topeka, that’s quite small. We only have 11 classes in the entire building. That intimacy—seeing students daily, learning every name—has been something really special.”

This fall, students from Shaner, Bishop, and Avondale West Elementary will come together to form the new Jardine Academy.

World production of major foods set records last year, according to this week’s outlook analysis from the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD).
Cereal stock levels have climbed to all-time highs.
A joint outlook prepared by the OECD and the United Nation’s Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) predicts weakening growth in global demand for agricultural commodities and food, while anticipating continuing productivity improvements in the sector.
As a result, prices of main agricultural commodities are expected to remain low for the next 10 years.
The report attributes the demand slowdown to a deceleration of demand growth in major emerging economies, stagnating per capita consumption of staple foods and a further gradual decline in global population growth rates.
The global agricultural and fish production is projected to grow by around 20 per cent over the coming decade, but with considerable variation across regions.
Strong growth is expected in developing regions with more rapid population growth, including Sub-Saharan Africa, South and East Asia, and the Middle East and North Africa. By contrast, production growth is expected to be much lower in developed countries, especially in Western Europe.
Declining demand growth for meat products will put a brake on the demand for cereals and protein meal used in animal feed.
With slower consumption and production growth, agricultural and fish trade are projected to grow at about half the rate of the previous decade.
Net exports are expected to increase from land-abundant countries, such as Canada and the Americas.
Countries with high population growth, in particular in the Middle East and North Africa, Sub-Saharan Africa and in Asia, will see rising net imports.
Demand for cereals and vegetable oil for the production of biofuels is expected to be largely unchanged over the forecast period, in contrast with the past decade, when biofuels expansion led to more than 120 million tonnes of additional cereals demand, predominantly corn.
With existing policies in developed countries unlikely to support biofuels expansion, most demand growth will come from developing countries that have introduced policies favouring biofuel use.
In particular, the use of sugarcane for biofuel production is expected to increase.
rewrite:
Global production of major food commodities reached record levels last year, as highlighted in a recent outlook analysis from the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD). Cereal stocks, in particular, have risen to unprecedented highs. A joint report by the OECD and the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) forecasts a slowdown in the growth of worldwide demand for agricultural products and food, even as productivity in the sector continues to improve. Consequently, prices for key agricultural commodities are projected to stay low over the coming decade.

This anticipated weakening in demand stems from several factors: a moderation in demand growth within major emerging economies, stagnant per capita consumption of staple foods, and a gradual, ongoing decline in global population growth rates. Overall, global agricultural and fisheries output is expected to expand by roughly 20 percent in the next ten years, though growth rates will vary significantly by region. Developing regions with faster population increases—such as Sub-Saharan Africa, South and East Asia, and the Middle East and North Africa—are likely to see strong production growth. In contrast, growth in developed countries, especially in Western Europe, is forecast to be far more modest.

A slowdown in the demand growth for meat products will, in turn, curb demand for cereals and protein meals used in animal feed. As both consumption and production expand more slowly, agricultural and fish trade is projected to grow at approximately half the pace of the previous decade. Net exports are expected to rise from land-abundant nations like those in the Americas and Canada. Meanwhile, regions with high population growth—notably the Middle East and North Africa, Sub-Saharan Africa, and parts of Asia—will experience increasing net imports.

Demand for cereals and vegetable oils used in biofuel production is predicted to remain largely stable over the forecast period. This marks a shift from the past decade, when biofuel expansion drove an additional demand of over 120 million tonnes of cereals, mainly corn. Given that existing policies in developed countries are unlikely to further support biofuel expansion, most future demand growth will originate in developing nations that have implemented policies favoring biofuel use. Specifically, the use of sugarcane for biofuel production is anticipated to rise.

General News of Friday, 6 October 2017
Source: Starrfmonline.com
2017-10-06
Sophia Akuffo, Chief Justice
The Chief Justice Sophia Akuffo has bemoaned the growing indiscipline at the BAR of Ghana as she charges newly enrolled lawyers to be of good behaviour.
According to Justice Akuffo, the high level of indiscipline amongst lawyers in Ghana is alarming and disappointing.
Addressing 208 newly enrolled lawyers to the Ghana BAR at the enrollment ceremony held at the Banquet Hall of the State House Friday, the Chief Justice said the Disciplinary Committee of the General Legal Council (GLC) is overwhelmed by the several misconduct complaints against lawyers.
She charged the newly enrolled lawyers to uphold all the rules governing the Profession they have chosen.
“We are witnessing these days a distressing increase in a number of disciplinary complaints that come before the disciplinary committee of the General Legal Council against lawyers especially the younger ones at the BAR.
“The root cause of most of these is lack of self-discipline and the desire to get rich quick on the part of new lawyers,” the Chief Justice said on Friday.
Justice Akuffo called on the lawyers to at all times observe the rules and ensure that none of them ever appears before the disciplinary committee of the General Legal Council.
rewrite:
Chief Justice Sophia Akuffo has expressed deep concern over the rising indiscipline within the Ghanaian Bar, urging newly enrolled lawyers to uphold high standards of conduct. Speaking at an enrollment ceremony at the State House Banquet Hall on Friday, she addressed 208 new lawyers, describing the current level of misconduct among legal practitioners as both alarming and disappointing.

Justice Akuffo noted that the Disciplinary Committee of the General Legal Council is inundated with complaints against lawyers, particularly younger members of the Bar. She emphasized that this troubling trend stems largely from a lack of self-discipline and a "get-rich-quick" mentality among some new entrants to the profession.

The Chief Justice charged the newly enrolled lawyers to strictly adhere to all professional rules and to maintain integrity in their practice. She urged them to conduct themselves in a manner that ensures they never face disciplinary proceedings. Her message underscored the importance of ethical behavior in preserving the dignity and trust of the legal profession in Ghana.
